# You don't have three problems

Source: https://lowob.com/research/you-dont-have-three-problems/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-02 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Fundraising, community and customer acquisition are three outputs of one commercial system. Teams that run them as separate projects pay for the same work three times and end up with a story nobody believes. Start with a named buyer, keep one evidence log, and sequence the raise, the community and the pipeline against each other.

Fundraising, community and customer acquisition are three outputs of one commercial system. Teams that run them as separate projects pay for the same work three times and still end up with a story nobody believes. The three depend on each other in a fixed order: a named buyer, early evidence from that buyer, a community that produces more of that evidence cheaply, and a round that funds distribution. In 2026 the order matters more, because capital is concentrating and investors are spending their limited reading time on traction.

## Why it splits

It splits because each one has a different audience and a different scoreboard. Investors want a market and a team. Communities want something to belong to. Customers want a problem solved. So founders write three stories.

The scoreboards are real, and they pull in different directions. Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev surveyed almost 900 venture capitalists for their study of how VCs decide. The team was named as important by 95% of firms and as the single most important factor by 47%. The business model was named by 83%, the product by 74% and the market by 68%. The average firm screened about 200 companies to make four investments a year. Customers keep a different score. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience, which means the customer story increasingly has to work on a website, in a forwarded document or in an AI summary, with nobody from the company present.

| Audience | Scoreboard | What they need to see | What usually gets shown instead |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Investors | Can this be large, and will this team win it? | A named buyer, early evidence, a credible next milestone | Market size and a vision slide |
| Community | Is being here early worth something real? | A role, access, recognition, a visible say | Hints about a token or a feature |
| Customers | Does it solve my problem, safely, for someone like me? | Peer proof, clear terms, a pilot | The raise and the investors' logos |

In web3 the split is worse, because the token often makes the investor, the community member and the customer the same person. In AI the split shows up differently: the investor story is about the model or the data, while the customer only cares whether the thing works on Tuesday.

Either way, you end up with a pitch deck that promises a market, a community that has been promised a token or a feature, and a customer pipeline that hasn't heard either promise.

## The dependency nobody draws

The three are not parallel. They depend on each other in a specific order.

1. **A named buyer comes first.** Not a market size, a person with a budget and a reason to act now.
2. **Early evidence from that buyer** (a pilot, a design partner, a letter of intent, a usage curve) is what the round is actually priced on.
3. **The community is where you manufacture that evidence cheaply:** testers, contributors, referrers, the first public advocates.
4. **The round funds the distribution** that turns early evidence into repeatable revenue.

Most teams try to run step 4 first. They raise on narrative, spend on distribution, and then go looking for the buyer the money was supposed to reach.

The funding market has made that shortcut more expensive. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, as reported by SiliconANGLE in July 2026, found US venture deal value reached $412.7 billion in the first half of 2026, with AI companies taking about 86%. Rounds of $100 million or more took 87.5% of the value. Deals under $100 million drew $51.4 billion, or 12.5%, down from 43.8% in 2024. For a company raising an ordinary round, that is a smaller pool and a more selective reader.

What that reader looks at has shifted too. DocSend, which tracks how investors view decks on its platform, reported that average seed-deck viewing time fell below two minutes in 2023 for the first time, while time spent on traction slides rose 33% at seed and 25% at pre-seed. Treat these as platform data from a vendor rather than a survey of all investors. The direction is consistent with the dependency above: the evidence from step 2 is what gets read. Our piece on [raising against evidence](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) sets out how to build the log that supplies it.

> Most teams raise on narrative, spend on distribution, and then go looking for the buyer the money was supposed to reach.

## What it looks like when it goes wrong

Two patterns come up again and again. Both are composites, described without names.

A crypto lending product ships a dozen new markets in a month. The product objection disappears overnight. The deposits don't move. Every problem left is downstream of distribution, and none of the three workstreams was pointed at it.

An AI product has the opposite problem: real usage, happy customers, and a fundraising story about the model rather than the customers. Investors keep asking for the thing the team already has, because the deck doesn't lead with it.

Same mistake in both. The story for one audience was built without the evidence from the other two. In the first case the community and the raise had been fed a product story while the buyer's real objection was trust and reach. In the second the customer evidence existed but lived in the sales team's notes, not in the deck.

## What changes when you run it as one system

**One product truth.** A single sentence about what this is and who buys it. Each audience gets its own belief to hold, but they all derive from the same truth. [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) shows how to write it.

**One evidence log.** Every pilot, quote, usage number and community contribution goes in one place, because every audience needs some of it.

**One calendar.** The raise, the community moments and the customer pushes are sequenced against each other, not run on three clocks.

**One owner.** Someone owns the order, even if three people do the work.

| Element | What it holds | Who draws on it | What happens without it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product truth | What it is, who buys it, why now | Deck, homepage, community posts, sales calls | Three stories that contradict each other |
| Evidence log | Dated pilots, quotes, usage, contributions, with source | Investors, customers, community | The best proof sits in one team's notes |
| Calendar | Raise milestones, community moments, customer pushes | Founders, community lead, sales | A launch lands the week the round goes quiet |
| Owner | The sequence and the trade-offs between audiences | Everyone | Each workstream optimises its own scoreboard |

The cost of running them apart is not only duplicated work. Gartner's June 2025 survey of 632 buyers found 69% reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them. A customer who hears one story from the site, another from the founder and a third from the community channel discounts all three. The same applies to an investor who checks the community before taking a second meeting.

The first audience in the sequence is also the hardest to pick. Our guides on [what a go-to-market strategy is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/) and [segment selection with evidence](https://lowob.com/research/segment-selection-with-evidence/) cover how to choose the named buyer from data rather than ambition.

Illustrative example: one log, three uses

Decision
:   Merge the investor update, the community changelog and the sales case notes into one dated evidence log owned by a single founder.

Reason and owner
:   The team found its strongest proof, a design partner's measured time saving, appeared in sales notes but not in the deck or the community channel. Owned by the co-founder running commercial work.

What changed
:   The design partner result moved to slide 2 of the deck, became the community's first "built with" post and went into the outbound sequence as the reason to talk.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage B2B software company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the buyer before the market.** A person with a budget and a reason to act now comes first, not a market size.
- **Price the round on evidence.** Pilots, design partners and usage curves are what investors read, and the reading window is short.
- **Give the community a job.** It is where you manufacture evidence cheaply, through testers, contributors and referrers.
- **Run one of each.** One product truth, one evidence log, one calendar and one owner.

Gateway card

### The one-system checklist

- You can name the buyer, not the market
- There is one sentence all three audiences could repeat back
- The deck leads with the best evidence customers and community have produced
- The community has a job beyond waiting for news
- You know what the first $100K after the round buys
